--- title: "Lesson 6 · Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests" subtitle: "Part I · Foundations" description: "Coverage of confidence intervals, p-values, errors and power, multiple testing, and evidence of absence." --- ::: {.meta-pills} [About 3 hours]{} [Before this: Lessons 4–5]{} [Threads: uncertainty · frequentist ↔ Bayesian]{} ::: ::: {.objectives} By the end of this lesson you will be able to - interpret a confidence interval through its coverage across repeated studies; - explain what a p-value is, and list what it is not; - describe type I and type II errors and calculate power; - explain why small studies that reach significance exaggerate effects; - control false positives when testing many hypotheses, and know when not to; - use an equivalence test to support "no meaningful effect". ::: ::: {.why} **Why it matters.** Confidence intervals and p-values are reported in almost every epidemiological paper, and misread in many of them. "Not significant" read as "no effect" has buried real harms; a single p < 0.05 from a small study has launched false alarms. The aim of this lesson is to make you a careful reader and writer of both. ::: ## 6.1 Confidence intervals and coverage {#s1} Each simulated study draws a sample of children and computes a 95% confidence interval for the risk of asthma. The true risk in the whole cohort is known. A 95% interval comes from a procedure that, across many studies, captures the truth 95% of the time. Any single interval either contains it or doesn't. Run 100 studies and count the misses. ```{=html}
interval contains the truthinterval missestrue risk
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$\hat\pi \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat\pi(1-\hat\pi)}{n}}$$ $$P_\pi\big(L \le \pi \le U\big) = 1 - \alpha \ \text{ for every } \pi$$ ::: {.note} $z_{0.975} = 1.96$ for a 95% interval. The probability statement is about the procedure, over repeated samples. ::: :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r smp <- cohort |> slice_sample(n = 200) p <- mean(smp$asthma) se <- sqrt(p * (1 - p) / 200) p + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se binom.test(sum(smp$asthma), 200)$conf.int ``` :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#ciReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Common pitfall"} "There is a 95% probability that the true risk lies between 9% and 18%." For a confidence interval, the 95% describes the method, not this interval. The statement in quotes is what a Bayesian credible interval says (Lesson 19). ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @gardner1986confidence argued for reporting confidence intervals rather than p-values; @greenland2016statistical list common misinterpretations of intervals; @kirkwood2003essential derive intervals for risks and rates. ::: ## 6.2 Hypothesis tests and p-values {#s2} A test asks: if there were truly no effect, how surprising would data like ours be? The **p-value** is the probability, computed under the null hypothesis, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. To see its behavior, run many studies comparing asthma risk between two groups. First use a fake "exposure" assigned by coin toss, so the null is true; then the real exposure, high modeled NO₂. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$H_0: \pi_1 = \pi_0 \quad\text{vs}\quad H_1: \pi_1 \ne \pi_0$$ $$z = \frac{\hat\pi_1 - \hat\pi_0}{\sqrt{\bar\pi(1-\bar\pi)\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_0}\right)}}, \qquad p = 2\,P(Z \ge |z|)$$ :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r smp <- cohort |> slice_sample(n = 500) |> mutate(high = no2_modeled >= 30) prop.test(table(smp$high, smp$asthma)[, 2:1], correct = FALSE) ``` :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#pvReport} ::: {.note} Report the effect estimate with its confidence interval and the exact p-value, not only "p < 0.05". ::: :::: ::::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false" title="R code (optional): p-values under the null and under a real effect"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(6) one_study <- function(n, real = TRUE) { smp <- slice_sample(cohort, n = n) expo <- if (real) smp$no2_modeled >= 30 else runif(n) < 0.5 prop.test(c(sum(smp$asthma[expo]), sum(smp$asthma[!expo])), c(sum(expo), sum(!expo)), correct = FALSE)$p.value } p_null <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) one_study(500, real = FALSE)) p_real <- map_dbl(1:1000, \(i) one_study(500, real = TRUE)) c(null_below_0.05 = mean(p_null < 0.05), real_below_0.05 = mean(p_real < 0.05)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> null_below_0.05 real_below_0.05 #> 0.048 0.258 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @wasserstein2016asa is the American Statistical Association's statement on p-values; @greenland2016statistical explain 25 common misinterpretations; @matthews1996interaction on comparing effect sizes rather than p-values. ::: ## 6.3 Errors, power and exaggerated estimates {#s3} Rejecting a true null is a **type I error**, with probability α. Missing a real effect is a **type II error**. **Power** is the probability of detecting an effect of a given size, and it depends on the effect, the baseline risk, the sample size and α. Small studies have low power, and there is a second, less obvious problem: when a low-powered study does reach significance, its estimate tends to be far too large. ```{=html}
``` ::: {.callout-warning title="Common pitfall"} Treating a significant result from a small study as a reliable estimate of the effect. Among the studies that pass p < 0.05, the estimates are biased upward, often severely. This "winner's curse" is one reason early findings shrink when replicated. ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @button2013power show how low power undermines reliability, including the exaggeration of significant effects; @greenland2016statistical on misinterpretations of power; @kirkwood2003essential give sample size and power calculations for epidemiological comparisons. ::: ## 6.4 Multiple testing {#s4} Test twenty exposures that have no effect at all, each at α = 0.05, and you expect one "significant" result by chance alone. The chance of at least one false positive is 64%. A Bonferroni correction divides α by the number of tests, at a cost in power. Whether to correct depends on the question: confirming a single pre-specified hypothesis, or exploring many. ```{=html}
``` ::::: {.triad} :::: {.a} ::: {.lab} [A]{.k}Standard notation ::: $$P(\text{at least one false positive}) = 1 - (1-\alpha)^m$$ $$\text{Bonferroni: reject } H_{0j} \text{ if } p_j < \alpha / m$$ :::: :::: {.b} ::: {.lab} [B]{.k}Model list and R ::: ```r p_values <- c(0.003, 0.02, 0.04, 0.30) p.adjust(p_values, method = "bonferroni") p.adjust(p_values, method = "holm") ``` :::: :::: {.c} ::: {.lab} [C]{.k}How it's reported ::: [ ]{#mtReport} :::: ::::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @bender2001adjusting explain when and how to adjust for multiple testing; @rothman1990no argues that adjustment is often unnecessary when results are interpreted with care; @greenland2016statistical place both views in context. ::: ## 6.5 Absence of evidence and equivalence {#s5} A non-significant result means the data are compatible with no effect. They may also be compatible with a large effect. "Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence." To support the claim that an effect is negligible, set a margin in advance, here a risk ratio between 0.9 and 1.1, and check whether the confidence interval lies entirely inside it. Move the estimate and its precision and watch the four possible conclusions. ```{=html}
``` ::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Bayesian preview"} A frequentist test can reject "no effect" but can never support it; that needs the separate equivalence test above. A Bayesian analysis can state the probability that the effect lies inside the margin (a "region of practical equivalence"), and a Bayes factor can weigh "no effect" against "some effect" directly. Lesson 23 compares the approaches. ::: ::: {.further} **Further reading:** @altman1995absence on why a non-significant result is not evidence of no effect; @lakens2017equivalence is a practical primer on equivalence tests (TOST); @greenland2016statistical on interpreting non-significant results. ::: ## Check your understanding {#quiz} ```{=html}
``` ## Key takeaways {#take} - A 95% confidence interval comes from a procedure that captures the truth in 95% of studies. Its width shows precision. - A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme if the null were true. It is not the probability that the null is true, nor a measure of effect size. - Under a true null, p-values are uniformly distributed: 5% fall below 0.05 by chance. - Power depends on effect size, baseline risk, sample size and α. Significant results from low-powered studies exaggerate effects. - Testing many hypotheses inflates false positives; correct when confirming, interpret carefully when exploring. - Non-significant does not mean no effect. To support "no meaningful effect", use an equivalence margin. ```{=html}
